title: Seven Woes and a Lament over Jerusalem
summary: Speaking to the crowds and his disciples, Jesus tells them to observe what the scribes and Pharisees teach from Moses but not to imitate what they do, and he forbids his followers the titles of rank, since the greatest must be a servant. He then pronounces seven woes on the scribes and Pharisees for hypocrisy, misplaced priorities, and the killing of the prophets, and ends with a lament over Jerusalem, whose house will be left desolate until it welcomes the one who comes in the name of the Lord.
story:
Jesus has silenced every group of questioners in the temple courts (22:46). Now he speaks about them rather than to them, in his last public teaching in Matthew. The chapter closes his public ministry: after it he leaves the temple and speaks only to his disciples, first about the temple's coming destruction (chapter 24) and then about readiness for his return and the last judgment (chapter 25). Many readers take chapters 23 to 25 together as the fifth of Matthew's great discourses, which ends with the formula ‘When Jesus had finished saying all these things’ (26:1); others treat chapter 23 as a public speech that stands on its own before the private teaching on the Mount of Olives.

The woes answer the leaders' rejection of Jesus with a prophetic verdict, and the lament at the end shows that the verdict is spoken with grief. The chapter also looks both ways in Matthew's story. It echoes the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus warned against righteousness done to be seen (6:1-18) and demanded a righteousness greater than that of the scribes and Pharisees (5:20). And its last words about the desolate house lead straight into chapter 24, where the disciples point out the temple's buildings and Jesus says not one stone will be left on another.
historical:
The scribes were trained interpreters and teachers of the Law of Moses, and many of them in Jesus' day belonged to the Pharisees, a lay movement devoted to applying the Law carefully to all of life, including purity and tithing, and to the traditions of earlier teachers. Josephus, who says he followed the Pharisees' way in public life (Life 12), describes them as the most accurate interpreters of the Law (Jewish War 2.162), as keepers of the traditions of the fathers not written in Moses (Antiquities 13.297), and as so influential with ordinary people that prayers and sacrifices were performed according to their teaching (Antiquities 18.15). They were respected, not the ruling elite, who were the high priestly families. Paul was a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5, Acts 23:6); Gamaliel, a Pharisee in the council, counseled restraint toward the apostles (Acts 5:34-39); some Pharisees warned Jesus that Herod meant to kill him (Luke 13:31); Nicodemus was one (John 3:1). After the temple fell in AD 70, the sages gathered at Yavneh under Yohanan ben Zakkai, heirs of the Pharisees, began to shape what became rabbinic Judaism, and many scholars read Matthew, written on the majority view in the following decades, as a rival claim to Israel's heritage made in that same moment (see the introduction).

The Pharisees' own heirs were blunt about hypocrisy. The Mishnah lists ‘the blows of the Pharisees’ among the things that wear out the world (m. Sotah 3:4). The Babylonian Talmud expands this into seven kinds of Pharisee, five of them caricatures of display, among them the ‘shoulder Pharisee’ who carries his good deeds on his shoulder to be seen, and it remembers King Alexander Jannaeus telling his wife on his deathbed to fear neither the Pharisees nor their opponents but the painted ones who imitate the Pharisees, whose deeds are like Zimri's and who seek the reward of Phinehas (b. Sotah 22b). Criticism of religious show was not Jesus' invention; it was part of Israel's own conscience.

Moses' seat (verse 2) is a phrase found nowhere earlier. The earliest Jewish text to use it, the Pesikta de Rav Kahana (1:7), a homiletic midrash from the Byzantine period, speaks of a teaching seat like the cathedra of Moses. Stone seats have been found in synagogues: a basalt chair discovered in 1926 at Chorazin, one of the Galilean towns Jesus rebuked (11:21), carries an Aramaic inscription remembering one Yudan son of Ishmael as a donor and is now in the Israel Museum; another comes from Hammath Tiberias; and a marble chair stands in the building on the Aegean island of Delos, excavated by André Plassart in 1912 to 1913 and identified by many, though not all, as a synagogue of the first or second century BC. The Galilean seats are later than Jesus, from the synagogues of the third to fifth centuries, so the phrase may name a real piece of furniture, a figure of speech for teaching authority, or both. Mark Allan Powell (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1995) argued that it refers to the scribes' and Pharisees' social position as those who controlled access to the Torah scrolls and read them to the people, so that Jesus tells the crowds to heed what they read from Moses rather than everything they teach.

Verse 15 has been read as evidence of Pharisaic mission to Gentiles. Josephus tells how Izates, king of Adiabene, was taught by a Jewish merchant named Ananias, who advised him not to be circumcised, until a Galilean named Eleazar, known for his strictness in the Law, persuaded him that he must (Antiquities 20.34-48). Horace's joke about poets who, like the Jews, compel people to join their crowd (Satires 1.4.142-143) is often cited too, though its meaning is disputed. Scot McKnight (A Light Among the Gentiles, 1991) and Martin Goodman (Mission and Conversion, 1994) persuaded many scholars that Second Temple Judaism was not a missionary religion in the Christian sense, so the woe may target zeal to turn Gentile sympathizers into full proselytes rather than a general campaign.

Verse 35 names the first and last murders in the Hebrew Bible when it is read in the order that ends with Chronicles: Abel (Genesis 4:8-10) and the priest Zechariah, stoned in the temple court for rebuking king and people, who cried as he died, ‘May the LORD see and avenge’ (2 Chronicles 24:20-22). The Babylonian Talmud gives that order for the Writings (b. Bava Batra 14b), though the great Tiberian codices of Aleppo and Leningrad put Chronicles first. Chronicles calls this Zechariah the son of Jehoiada; Matthew says son of Berechiah, the father of the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1), a difficulty taken up in the hard questions.
cultural:
Many details reflect daily religious practice. Phylacteries (tefillin) were small leather cases holding passages of Scripture, bound on the arm and forehead in obedience to Deuteronomy 6:8 and 11:18 and Exodus 13:9 and 13:16; examples have been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Tassels (tzitzit) were fringes on the four corners of a garment, commanded in Numbers 15:38-39 and Deuteronomy 22:12 as a reminder of God's commandments. Jesus himself wore them: the woman with the flow of blood touched the kraspedon of his cloak (9:20), the word used here. His complaint is not about tefillin or tassels but about enlarging them for show. The places of honor at banquets were the couches nearest the host, the chief seats in the synagogue faced the congregation, and greetings in the marketplace meant being hailed with titles of respect. ‘Rabbi’, literally ‘my great one’, was a respectful address for a teacher in Jesus' day and became a formal title for ordained sages after AD 70. The Mishnah remembers the sage Shemaiah teaching his disciples to love work and hate lordship (m. Avot 1:10), and it calls Hillel and Shammai the fathers of the world (m. Eduyot 1:4), which shows how naturally teachers were called father; the tractate of sayings is itself called Avot, ‘Fathers’.

The oath formulas in verses 16 to 22 reflect a real concern to protect the divine name by swearing by something connected to God instead. The Mishnah exempts from liability an oath ‘by heaven and by earth’ while holding binding one sworn by the divine names or their substitutes (m. Shevuot 4:13), and Philo advises that if one must swear, one should swear by something less than God, such as earth, sun, or heaven (Special Laws 2.2-5). Jesus had already forbidden evasive oaths altogether (5:33-37); here he argues that every such oath still reaches the God who dwells in the temple and sits on heaven's throne.

The Law required a tithe of the produce of the land, grain, wine, and oil above all (Leviticus 27:30, Deuteronomy 14:22-23). Pharisaic practice extended it to kitchen herbs: the Mishnah lists cumin among foods to be tithed everywhere (m. Demai 2:1) and records Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that dill must be tithed in seed, leaves, and pods (m. Maaserot 4:5). Jesus approves the practice (‘without neglecting the former’) but names the weightier matters, justice, mercy, and faithfulness, which echo Micah 6:8 and Hosea 6:6, the verse Matthew has quoted twice (9:13, 12:7). Straining wine through cloth kept out tiny insects, which were unclean (Leviticus 11:41-43), while the camel was the largest unclean animal in the land (Leviticus 11:4). Many have noticed that in Aramaic the words for gnat (qalma) and camel (gamla) sound alike.

Purity rules distinguished the outside and the inside of vessels (m. Kelim 25:1), and the schools of Hillel and Shammai debated related questions (m. Berakhot 8:2). Jacob Neusner argued (New Testament Studies, 1976) that the saying about cleaning the inside of the cup presupposes just such a debate, and turns it into a call to cleanse the heart. Tombs were marked with lime (m. Maaser Sheni 5:1), and the marks were renewed each spring on the fifteenth of Adar, before the pilgrims arrived for Passover (m. Shekalim 1:1), so that no one would touch a grave by accident and contract the seven-day impurity of Numbers 19:16. The white paint that warned of death is Jesus' picture of a righteous surface over an unclean heart; Paul later calls a high priest a whitewashed wall (Acts 23:3). Monumental tombs lined the Kidron Valley opposite the temple, among them the monolith now called the Tomb of Zechariah and the tomb of the priestly family of Hezir, and Josephus says Herod built a costly monument of white stone at the entrance to David's tomb (Antiquities 16.182). The Lives of the Prophets, a Jewish work of the first century preserved by Christians, records where the prophets were buried and how some were killed, and Joachim Jeremias (Heiligengräber in Jesu Umwelt, 1958) studied the cult of saints' tombs in Jesus' world. Gehenna, translated hell, was the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, once a site of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31), which had become the name for final judgment.
literary:
The chapter has three movements: a warning to the crowds and disciples (verses 1 to 12), seven woes addressed directly to the scribes and Pharisees (verses 13 to 36, counting without the omitted verse 14), and a lament over Jerusalem (verses 37 to 39). Luke has similar woes at a Pharisee's table, three against Pharisees and three against experts in the law (Luke 11:37-52), and places the lament elsewhere (Luke 13:34-35); Mark has only a brief warning about the scribes (Mark 12:38-40). Matthew gathers the material into one great speech. A woe (ouai) is a prophetic form, a cry of grief and doom together, familiar from Isaiah 5:8-23 and Habakkuk 2:6-19, where woes also come in series. Many readers see the seven woes as a dark counterpart to the Beatitudes at the start of Jesus' teaching (5:3-12): the ministry opens with blessings on the poor in spirit and the merciful and closes with woes on those who neglect mercy.

The woes are built with care. Each begins with the same formula, ‘Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites’, except the third, which begins ‘Woe to you, blind guides’; blindness is the chapter's second refrain (verses 16, 17, 19, 24, 26), picking up Jesus' earlier word that the Pharisees are blind guides of the blind (15:14). The images move from outside to inside: broad phylacteries, the outside of the cup, whitewashed tombs. The sequence also climbs, from hindering others (verse 13) and misleading converts (15), through casuistry about oaths (16 to 22) and tithing that forgets justice (23 to 24), to inner corruption (25 to 28), and finally to complicity in murder (29 to 36). The accusation that they are sons of those who killed the prophets turns on a Semitic idiom, where ‘son of’ means one who shares a character; by claiming they would not have joined their fathers, they admit their fathers did it.

The last woe widens into an oracle of judgment. Jesus speaks in the first person as the one who sends ‘prophets and wise men and teachers’ (verse 34), and the phrase ‘all these things will come upon this generation’ (verse 36) anticipates the same solemn formula in the next chapter (24:34). Then the tone breaks. The speech that began with a seat of authority ends with a hen and her chicks, and with a quotation of Psalm 118:26, the psalm the crowds sang at his entry (21:9), “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.” The verb for gathering (episunagō) in verse 37 returns in 24:31, when the Son of Man gathers his elect: what Jerusalem refused, the Son of Man will still do.

outline.t: Do what they teach, not what they do; the greatest is a servant
Woes for shutting the kingdom and corrupting converts
Woe for neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness
Woes for outward cleanness and inward corruption
Woe for honoring the prophets and killing them

doctrines.note: Jesus forbids his followers titles that set some above the rest, because they have one Teacher, one Father in heaven, and one Instructor, the Christ, and are all brothers (verses 8 to 10). The greatest must be a servant (verse 11). The warning is aimed at leaders who bind burdens on others, love honor, and perform for an audience, and it applies to Christian leaders at least as sharply as to the scribes and Pharisees.

Jesus neither dismisses the Law nor its careful keeping: the scribes' teaching from Moses is to be heeded (verse 3), and tithes of herbs should not be neglected (verse 23). But the Law has weightier matters, justice, mercy, and faithfulness, and the teacher who strains the small while swallowing the great has misread the whole. This is the same Jesus who hung the Law and the Prophets on love (22:40).

Holiness begins with the inside. Clean cups full of greed and whitewashed tombs full of bones picture a religion that manages appearances. First clean the inside, Jesus says, so that the outside may become clean as well (verse 26); outward practice is meant to be the fruit of a cleansed heart, not a substitute for it.

The woes announce that the generation that rejects God's final messengers will bear the weight of all the righteous blood shed before (verses 35 and 36). Judgment here is spoken by a prophet who weeps over the city he condemns, and it comes as the fulfillment of a long history of refusal, not as a sudden outburst.

The lament shows God's love for Jerusalem in Jesus' own voice: how often he longed to gather her children. The house is left desolate, as Jeremiah warned (Jeremiah 22:5), yet the last word looks ahead to a day when Jerusalem will say, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord” (verse 39). Christians differ on how that hope will be fulfilled, but the chapter ends with longing, not rejection.

words.note: Hupokritēs, hypocrite. In classical Greek it meant an actor, one who answers or plays a part on stage, and by extension a pretender. It occurs seventeen times in the New Testament in the critical text, thirteen in Matthew, six of them in this chapter's woes, and the related noun hupokrisis appears in verse 28. Jesus uses it for people whose religious life is a performance for an audience, where the face shown and the heart within do not match (6:2, 6:5, 6:16). It can also carry the sense of one who is godless under a pious surface, as in the Greek Old Testament of Job (34:30, 36:13).

Ouai, woe, alas, an exclamation of pain or grief. It occurs about forty-six times in the New Testament, thirteen in Matthew, seven in this chapter. In the Greek Old Testament it renders the Hebrew hoy and oy of the prophets' laments and judgment oracles (Isaiah 5:8-23, Amos 6:1). It is not a curse that wishes harm but a grieving announcement of doom, and it can be spoken over those one loves, as Jesus speaks it over Chorazin and Bethsaida (11:21) and over the betrayer (26:24).

Kathedra, seat, chair. It occurs three times in the New Testament: the seats of the dove sellers in the temple (21:12, Mark 11:15) and Moses' seat here (verse 2). The Latin form gives English ‘cathedral’, a bishop's seat, and the phrase ex cathedra. The verb that goes with it, kathizō, ‘they sit’, can mean to take one's seat as a teacher (5:1, 26:55). Whether the seat was literal furniture or a figure for authority, Jesus grants that those who sit in it speak Moses to the people.

Kraspedon, edge, fringe, tassel. It occurs five times in the New Testament. In verse 5 it means the tzitzit, the tassels on a garment's corners commanded in Numbers 15:38-39, where the Greek Old Testament uses the same word. Elsewhere in Matthew it is the fringe of Jesus' own cloak that the sick touched for healing (9:20, 14:36). The contrast is telling: the same garment feature that carried healing on Jesus is lengthened for display by those who ‘do all their deeds to be seen’.

Kathēgētēs, guide, teacher, instructor. It occurs only here in the New Testament, twice in verse 10. In the Greek world it was used for a tutor or a philosopher's teacher, and in modern Greek it means professor. Jesus reserves it for himself: ‘you have one Instructor, the Christ.’ The three titles of verses 8 to 10, Rabbi, Father, Instructor, are each answered by one who alone deserves them, the Teacher, the Father in heaven, and the Christ.

Prosēlutos, proselyte, literally one who has come over. It occurs four times in the New Testament (here and Acts 2:10, 6:5, 13:43). In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew ger, the resident foreigner, and by the first century it had come to mean a Gentile who fully converted to Judaism, with circumcision for men. Acts names proselytes among the first believers, including Nicolaus of Antioch, one of the Seven (Acts 6:5).

Geenna, Gehenna, from the Hebrew name of the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem. It occurs twelve times in the New Testament, seven in Matthew, and only once outside the Gospels (James 3:6). In Jesus' teaching it stands for final judgment. That he uses it twice in this chapter of religious leaders, calling a convert a son of hell (verse 15) and asking how they will escape its sentence (verse 33), rather than of notorious sinners, is part of the chapter's shock.

Episunagō, to gather together. It occurs eight times in the New Testament, used of crowds gathering (Mark 1:33, Luke 12:1) and, in the Gospels' most important uses, of Jesus' longing to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks (verse 37, twice) and of the Son of Man sending his angels to gather his elect (24:31). The Greek Old Testament uses the verb and its relatives for God's promise to gather scattered Israel (Psalm 106:47, 2 Maccabees 2:18).

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus speaking with the authority of God himself. He is the one Teacher and the one Instructor, the Christ (verses 8 and 10), and he claims a title no rabbi could claim: the disciples are all brothers because they have one Master. He says, ‘I am sending you prophets and wise men and teachers’ (verse 34), as God sent the prophets in Israel's history (Jeremiah 7:25, 2 Chronicles 24:19). Luke's version of the saying attributes it to the Wisdom of God (Luke 11:49); Matthew puts it in Jesus' own mouth, one of the passages that has led many interpreters to see Matthew presenting Jesus as Wisdom in person (compare 11:19, 11:28-30).

In the lament he uses an image the Old Testament uses of God: sheltering his people under his wings (Deuteronomy 32:11; Psalm 17:8, 36:7, 57:1, 91:4; Ruth 2:12). ‘How often I have longed to gather your children’ is the voice of Israel's God, who had sent his messengers early and often (2 Chronicles 36:15-16). The one who speaks the woes is the one who weeps, and within days he will be the prophet killed in Jerusalem, the righteous blood shed there. Matthew is aware of the irony: the crowd will soon say of Jesus, “His blood be on us and on our children” (27:25), while the reader knows from the Last Supper that his blood is poured out for the forgiveness of sins (26:28). His blood does not cry for vengeance like Abel's, but speaks a better word (Hebrews 12:24).

The last line looks past his coming rejection. ‘You will not see Me again until you say’ the words of Psalm 118:26 points to his return, and interpreters differ whether it promises Jerusalem's welcome, warns of a recognition that will come too late, or states the condition on which he will come (Dale Allison argued for the last in the Journal for the Study of the New Testament, 1983). On any reading, the chapter ends not with a closed door but with the words of a festal psalm still waiting to be sung. Paul's hope that all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:26) stands nearby.
interpretation:
Matthew 23 has one of the darkest reception histories in the New Testament. From the patristic period on, Christian writers applied its woes, together with the crowd's cry in 27:25, “His blood be on us and on our children,” to the Jewish people as a whole, and Pharisee became a byword for hypocrite in European languages. John Chrysostom's eight sermons Against the Jews (Antioch, 386 to 387) drew on this language, and Luther's On the Jews and Their Lies (1543) urged violence against Jewish communities. Medieval passion plays and sermons, and centuries of Good Friday preaching, fed the charge of deicide. At the Reformation both sides also turned the woes on each other's clergy, reading the Pharisees as a picture of their opponents rather than themselves.

After the Holocaust that history came under judgment. The French Jewish historian Jules Isaac, whose wife and daughter died at Auschwitz, published Jésus et Israël (1948) documenting what he called the teaching of contempt; his proposals shaped the Ten Points of Seelisberg (1947), and his audience with Pope John XXIII on 13 June 1960 helped set in motion the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965), which taught that Christ's passion cannot be charged against all Jews then living or against Jews today, and that Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God. The Vatican's Notes on the Correct Way to Present the Jews and Judaism in Preaching and Catechesis (1985) added that an exclusively negative picture of the Pharisees is likely to be inaccurate and unjust. In 2019 the Pontifical Biblical Institute held a conference on the Pharisees, addressed by Pope Francis, published as The Pharisees, edited by Joseph Sievers and Amy-Jill Levine (2021).

Scholarship had begun the correction earlier. Claude Montefiore, a Jewish scholar, judged the chapter's violence unhistorical in his commentary The Synoptic Gospels (1909); the Unitarian scholar R. Travers Herford (The Pharisees, 1924) and George Foot Moore (Christian Writers on Judaism, Harvard Theological Review, 1921) exposed the caricatures in Christian scholarship; E. P. Sanders (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977) reshaped the field's picture of first-century Judaism. On the chapter itself, David Garland (The Intention of Matthew 23, 1979) argued that Matthew aimed it chiefly as a warning to the leaders of his own Christian community, and Luke Timothy Johnson (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1989) showed that its language matches the conventions of ancient polemic between rival schools, harsh by modern standards and not meant as a sociological description. Jewish readers such as Amy-Jill Levine have asked Christians to read the woes as a quarrel inside Israel and to preach them against themselves.

The chapter has other lives. Protestant polemic often read ‘call no one father’ against clerical titles, while Catholic and Orthodox readers note that Paul calls himself a father to his converts (1 Corinthians 4:15) and read the saying as forbidding rivalry with God, not all use of the word. ‘Whited sepulchre’ entered English from the King James Version; Joseph Conrad uses it in Heart of Darkness (1899) for the European city that ran the Congo trade. The traditional Western Gospel for St. Stephen's Day, 26 December, is 23:34-39, joining the first Christian martyr to the prophets killed in Jerusalem. The Revised Common Lectionary reads 23:1-12 on Proper 26 of Year A, and the Roman lectionary on the Thirty-first Sunday in Ordinary Time. The altar of the Franciscan church of Dominus Flevit on the Mount of Olives (Antonio Barluzzi, 1955) bears a mosaic of a hen gathering her chicks.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter.

Verse 14 is missing from the earliest and most important manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and Codex Bezae, and from early versions. It adds a woe on those who devour widows' houses and make long prayers for a pretense, and its words match Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47, and the manuscripts that include them place them in different positions, some before verse 13 and some after it (the Textus Receptus puts them after, which is why the King James Version numbers them 14). Editors conclude that a scribe added the woe from Mark or Luke, and modern Bibles print it in a note. With it Matthew has eight woes; without it, seven.

In verse 4 the words ‘and burdensome’ are absent from some manuscripts, and editions divide; Westcott and Hort and the SBL edition omit them. In verse 8 the King James Version reads ‘for one is your Master, even Christ’, where the earliest manuscripts have ‘one Teacher’ and no mention of Christ, which later scribes brought over from verse 10. In verse 19 the King James Version adds ‘fools and’ before blind. In verse 25 some manuscripts read ‘unrighteousness’ for ‘self-indulgence’. In verse 35 the words ‘son of Berechiah’ are missing from the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, a few other manuscripts, and quotations in Eusebius; they are secure in the rest of the tradition, and most scholars regard the omission as a scribal attempt to remove the difficulty. In verse 38 Codex Vaticanus and a few others lack ‘desolate’; the word may have been dropped as redundant after ‘left’ or added to match Jeremiah 22:5 in the Greek, and the editors of the United Bible Societies' text include it with considerable doubt. The King James Version's ‘strain at a gnat’ in verse 24 is an older English way of saying ‘strain out’, not a different Greek text.

teach.big: Jesus warns every religious leader and follower against a faith performed for an audience, which binds others and neglects justice, mercy, and faithfulness, and he speaks his judgment with the grief of God who longs to gather his people.

outline.t: Authority to teach God's word is real, but it does not excuse leaders who lay burdens on others, will not lift a finger, and do their deeds to be seen.
In Christ's community there is one Teacher, one Father, one Instructor; everyone else is a brother or sister, and greatness is measured by service.
The worst hypocrisy stands in the doorway of the kingdom and keeps others out, and zeal for converts can reproduce our own sins in them.
Every promise is made before God; clever distinctions that let us off our word do not change who hears it.
Careful obedience in small things is good, but it becomes absurd when it swallows justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
God looks at the inside; religion that manages its appearance while the heart stays greedy is a whitewashed tomb.
Honoring dead prophets is easy; the test is how we treat the living ones, and every generation is tempted to think it would have done better than its fathers.
Judgment is spoken with tears: Jesus longs to gather his people, grieves their refusal, and leaves the door open to a future welcome.

teach.pitfalls:
The first and gravest misuse is to read this chapter as a portrait of Jews or Judaism. It has been read that way for centuries, with terrible results, and a teacher should say so plainly. Jesus speaks as a Jew within Israel, in the tradition of the prophets, whose words to Israel's leaders were at least as severe (Jeremiah 7, Ezekiel 34); he tells the crowds to heed what the scribes read from Moses (verse 3); and the rabbinic sources themselves condemned hypocritical Pharisees. The Pharisees were not a byword for legalism in their own day but the most respected teachers of the people.

The second misuse is to point the chapter outward. Pharisee is not a label for the Christians we disagree with, the other denomination, or the other political side. Jesus addresses verses 8 to 12 to his own disciples, and the church has never lacked leaders who love the best seats, lay heavy loads, and manage appearances. The chapter is best preached as a mirror, with the preacher first in front of it.

Third, avoid the opposite error of treating careful obedience as the problem. Jesus says the tithes should be kept (verse 23); his target is not devotion but devotion that forgets justice and mercy. Fourth, do not flatten ‘call no one father’ into a rule about vocabulary. Christians have applied it differently, and its point is that no human teacher may take the place of God or Christ. Finally, do not end at the woes. The chapter ends with a hen gathering her chicks, and a sermon that leaves out the lament has misrepresented the speaker.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press hardest on people who have been harmed by religious leaders: those whose pastors laid heavy burdens and would not lift a finger, those shamed for small failures while leaders' greed went unchallenged, and survivors of spiritual abuse. They need to hear that Jesus saw this and named it, and that his anger was on their side. Teach it carefully in their presence; do not use the text to stir up contempt, but do not soften it into a general call to niceness. The scrupulous may hear every woe as an accusation and conclude they are hypocrites because they are imperfect. A hypocrite in this chapter is not someone who struggles and fails but someone who performs righteousness for an audience while refusing mercy to others. Where Jewish neighbors, friends, or family members are present or in view, name the chapter's misuse honestly and grieve it, as the church has learned to do.

hard.q: Is this chapter unfair to the Pharisees, and has it fed hostility toward Jews?
hard.a:
The objection is strong and should be heard at full strength. Jewish scholars since Claude Montefiore (The Synoptic Gospels, 1909) have argued that the chapter's portrait of the Pharisees is not merely harsh but historically false: the Pharisees' own heirs taught that God looks at the heart, condemned hypocrisy themselves (m. Sotah 3:4; b. Sotah 22b), and were far from the heartless formalists of Christian imagination. Many critical scholars add that the chapter reflects the bitter conflict between Matthew's community and the synagogues after AD 70 more than Jesus' own words, so that later quarrels have been placed in his mouth. And the history is damning. Read with the crowd's cry in 27:25, the woes were used for centuries to justify contempt, expulsion, and violence against Jews; John Chrysostom's sermons Against the Jews (386 to 387) and Luther's On the Jews and Their Lies (1543) are only the best-known examples, and Jules Isaac (Jésus et Israël, 1948) traced a direct line from such teaching of contempt to the Christian soil in which the Holocaust grew. On this view the chapter is not a mirror but a weapon.

The responses do not deny that history; they begin by grieving it. The Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate (1965) and the Vatican's 1985 Notes on preaching, together with many Protestant statements, have rejected any reading that presents Jews as rejected or accursed, or the Pharisees in a wholly negative light. Historically, Luke Timothy Johnson (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1989) showed that the chapter's invective follows the conventions of ancient polemic between rival schools, where Jews at Qumran and Greek philosophers used similar language against opponents, so it should not be read as sober description. Literarily, Jesus speaks as a Jewish prophet within Israel, affirms the Pharisees' reading of Moses (verse 3), targets practice and not the Law or the people, and turns the same warnings on his own followers (verses 8 to 12); David Garland (The Intention of Matthew 23, 1979) argued that Matthew meant the chapter chiefly as a warning to Christian leaders. The New Testament also names Pharisees who were sympathetic or who became believers, Nicodemus, Gamaliel, and Paul. Scholars still differ on how much of the chapter goes back to Jesus and how much reflects Matthew's setting. Christians who hold that these are Jesus' words can agree that he spoke them as Jeremiah spoke to Jerusalem, from inside and with tears, and that Christian readers who use them against Jews have turned the mirror into a stone. The chapter is rightly read when Christians find themselves in it first.

hard.q: Who was ‘Zechariah son of Berechiah’, and did Matthew confuse two different men?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real. The Zechariah who was murdered ‘between the temple and the altar’ in the Hebrew Bible is the priest Zechariah son of Jehoiada, stoned in the temple court in the reign of Joash, around 800 BC (2 Chronicles 24:20-22). Zechariah son of Berechiah is the prophet whose book stands among the Twelve, active around 520 BC (Zechariah 1:1), and the Old Testament says nothing of his death. Luke's parallel names only ‘Zechariah’ (Luke 11:51). Skeptical critics have long cited the verse as a plain error in Matthew, and many critical commentators, among them W. D. Davies and Dale Allison, agree that the evangelist or his tradition conflated the two men.

Several explanations have been offered since the early church. The first accepts a conflation but notes that Jewish tradition made the same one: the Aramaic Targum of Lamentations 2:20 names the priest and prophet killed in the sanctuary on the Day of Atonement as Zechariah son of Iddo, the prophet's grandfather (Zechariah 1:1), and the Babylonian Talmud tells how his blood seethed on the temple floor until Nebuzaradan avenged it (b. Gittin 57b, b. Sanhedrin 96b). On this view Matthew reflects a known identification, not a private slip. The second treats the patronymic as an early scribal gloss: it is absent from the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus and from Eusebius's quotations, and Jerome reports that the gospel used by the Nazarenes read ‘son of Joiada’ (Commentary on Matthew, on 23:35). The third proposes that Jehoiada had another name or that Berechiah was an ancestor, since son can mean descendant, though there is no evidence for either. The fourth identifies the man with Zechariah son of Baris (or Baruch), murdered by the Zealots ‘in the middle of the temple’ in AD 67 or 68 (Josephus, Jewish War 4.334-344), which would make the saying a prophecy or a later addition; most scholars reject this because Jesus speaks of a murder already done. A fifth, found in Origen and in the second-century Protevangelium of James (23-24), identifies him with Zechariah the father of John the Baptist, killed in the temple, according to that legend, by Herod's agents.

The point of the saying is clear on every view: from the first martyr in Genesis to the last in the book that closed the Hebrew canon as the rabbis ordered it, all the righteous blood comes to its reckoning. Christians who hold a high view of Scripture's truthfulness have favored the scribal, the double-name, or the traditional-identification solutions; others accept that Matthew followed a Jewish tradition that had already merged the two Zechariahs. This is a question about a detail of reference, and faithful readers differ about it.

observe: What does Jesus tell the crowds to do about the scribes' and Pharisees' teaching in verse 3, and what does he tell them not to do?
List the images Jesus uses in the woes (the cup, the tombs, the gnat and the camel). What does each contrast?
What image does Jesus use for himself in verse 37, and what does he say Jerusalem will one day say?
interpret: Why do you think Jesus forbids the titles Rabbi, Father, and Instructor among his followers? What is he protecting?
What makes justice, mercy, and faithfulness weightier than tithing herbs, and why does Jesus still say the tithes should not be neglected?
How does the lament in verses 37 to 39 change the way you hear the woes that come before it?
apply: Where are you tempted to practice your faith for an audience, and what would it look like to do the same thing unseen?
Jesus says the builders of prophets' tombs would have joined in killing them. Who are the living prophets you find easiest to honor only after they are gone?
How can your church read this chapter as a mirror for itself rather than a weapon against others?
